transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Time: 10:30 AM PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM), Maya Rodriguez (Quantaco Head of ML), Tom Ellis (Quantaco Infra), Priya Singh (Quantaco Product)

Summary (auto): weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ numbers, caching hit-rate impact, batching tradeoffs and next steps to run extended benchmarks and update pricing worksheet.

[00:00] Elena: alright everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, maya, priya, tom, you all see the benchmark sheet i sent?
[00:08] Maya: yeah just pulled it up, thanks elena. audio's good.
[00:12] Samir: cool, so agenda today — run through the numbers from last week's load test, talk about caching and batching trade-offs, and agree on next steps for the 24 hour run.
[00:22] Tom: perfect. we mainly want to understand tokens per dollar and latency impacts if we push batching.
[00:27] Elena: right, and we also included a model variant comparison — 8-bit quant vs 4-bit experimental — to see unit economics.
[00:34] Maya: quick qualifier, our production mix is ~65% short prompts (<=128 tokens), 30% medium (128-512) and 5% long (>512). most of the heavy tail is retrieval-augmented generation where caching should help.
[00:46] Samir: that distribution helps a lot. on our test cluster we kept seq len = 512 for a baseline, and ran continuous batching with target batch size 8 and dynamic batching up to 32.
[00:57] Priya: can you remind us the baseline tokens/sec and cost numbers? the sheet has a bunch.
[01:03] Samir: yeah quick numbers from the 1 hour synthetic run: on the 8-bit profile, single GPU sustained ~900 tokens/sec at p99 latency ~220ms for short tails. cost per GPU hour in our test env is modeled at $3.60, which gives a rough tokens/sec per dollar of about 250 tokens/sec/$. i know that metric is a little weird but it's helpful for comparing configs.
[01:27] Maya: 250 tokens/sec/$? earlier you mentioned higher numbers, is that with caching?
[01:32] Samir: good point. that's raw, no prefix caching. when we enable KV prefix caching with a 40% hit rate, effective tokens generated from model drops by ~35%, so tokens/sec/$ improves to ~380 tokens/sec/$. also batching more aggressively (target 16-24) pushes GPU utilization up and we saw ~20% throughput gain but latency tail degrades by ~30ms.
[01:56] Tom: what about the 4-bit profile? is it production safe?
[02:00] Samir: 4-bit gives ~1.8x throughput vs 8-bit in these runs, so tokens/sec/$ jumps to ~680 tokens/sec/$ raw. caveat: we saw some quality regressions on a few eval prompts (nonsensical repetitions). so it's promising for cost but needs eval gating.
[02:18] Maya: quality regressions are a hard no for our customer-facing assistant. we can consider 4-bit on internal-only pipelines, but not for user-facing until we have eval passes.
[02:27] Elena: that's consistent with other customers. the usual play is 8-bit for prod, 4-bit for batch/ingest/embedding precompute.
[02:35] Jordan: also worth mentioning that caching isn't just KV prefix. we can do request-level caching for identical prompts (useful for templates), and we estimate another ~8% savings there for your call volumes.
[02:46] Priya: how stable are these numbers across different sequence length mixes? our mix is skewed to short so maybe tokens/sec/$ would be higher in prod?
[02:54] Samir: yes — short sequences have much lower per-token compute overhead because of attention complexity scaling. when we re-weight tests to your distribution (65% short), tokens/sec/$ jumps to ~430 tokens/sec/$ on 8-bit with caching. on 4-bit with same distribution it's ~760 tokens/sec/$.
[03:12] Tom: latency constraints — our SLA is 250ms p95 for UI calls. do these batching choices keep us within that?
[03:18] Samir: with target batch 8 and dynamic up to 16 we were at p95 ~190ms on 8-bit for short/median. pushing batching to 32 got us to p95 ~240-260ms depending on mix, so borderline. for us we'd recommend dynamic batching with a strict p95 cap — Redwood supports fallbacks that route to a lower-batch path if latency approaches the SLO.
[03:39] Maya: can you explain the fallback behavior — like will requests reroute to hosted lower-latency pool automatically?
[03:44] Elena: yeah policy based — you can set latency SLOs and routing priorities. for example if Dedicated pool is full and latency climbing, requests can fallback to a hosted low-latency instance or a smaller model variant.
[03:55] Priya: ok good. back to cost math — elena you had a worksheet with line items?
[03:59] Elena: yes i shared a worksheet. top line assumptions: GPU cost $3.60/hr, avg tokens per request 120, requests per second target 8 RPS, desired p95 latency 250ms. worksheet does a per-feature calc: model cost, infra, caching savings, and amortized engineering overhead. it outputs cost per 1M tokens and tokens/sec/$.
[04:21] Tom: what's your 1M tokens cost number in the sheet?
[04:24] Elena: baseline 8-bit w/o caching is about $18 per 1M tokens. with 40% caching and batching optimizations that drops to $11 per 1M tokens. with 4-bit experimental that can drop to $6-7 per 1M but again quality caveats.
[04:39] Maya: $18 -> $11 is meaningful. is that aligned with dedicated pricing or hosted?
[04:44] Elena: those numbers assume Dedicated reserved pool economics. hosted API has slightly higher unit cost but includes overhead and reliability. we can run hybrid where hot routes go hosted and bulk goes dedicated.
[04:55] Samir: wanted to call out a micro-optimization we tried — KV cache TTL tuning. by increasing TTL from 5 minutes to 30 minutes for a subset of retrieval prompts we saw hit-rate move from 22% to 38%, which gave immediate 12% reduction in model token spend. downside is staler cache for very dynamic user prompts.
[05:15] Priya: for our use case most retrieval chunks are stable within a user session so longer TTL seems ok, but we need controls for privacy/scoped content.
[05:24] Maya: security question — are cache entries encrypted at rest and how do they handle multi-tenant isolation?
[05:29] Elena: yes cache stores can be customer-isolated in Private deployment; they can be encrypted with customer KMS. in hosted we encrypt at rest and have RBAC controls. we'll attach our security doc as requested.
[05:40] Tom: competitor question — how do these numbers compare to what we saw with Anthropic on our last benchmark?
[05:46] Samir: rough comparison: Anthropic endpoints achieved slightly lower p99 latency but higher unit cost by ~20% in their managed offering. AWS Bedrock had more variable performance depending on instance type. Run:AI was similar on utilization but you manage more infra overhead.
[06:01] Maya: okay, practical ask — can we see a 24 hour stability run with our real traffic replay and caching enabled? that's the only way we believe the tokens/sec/$ number.
[06:09] Elena: yes, that's in the plan. samir will run an extended replay on the dedicated pool with your distribution and caching TTLs you propose.
[06:16] Samir: plan is to run for 24 hours starting next monday window, collect p50/p95/p99 latency, KV hit-rates, GPU utilization, tokens emitted, and cost burn. i'll post a CSV and a summary slide.
[06:26] Priya: timeline? we need results before the exec review on 10/30.
[06:30] Samir: we'll run it by 10/27 and have a results deck by 10/29.
[06:34] Elena: great. a few other notes from the bench: prefix caching is most effective for multi-turn scenarios where the retrieval remains constant across turns — that gave us 60-70% per-session token savings in some demos. but it depends on your conversation patterns.
[06:51] Tom: what's the expected engineering lift to implement client-side caching TTL controls?
[06:55] Jordan: minimal — we expose TTL and scope flags in the SDK; quantaco's infra just needs to decide TTL per prompt type and pass headers.
[07:03] Maya: will you share a sample config?
[07:05] Elena: yes i'll attach sample SDK snippet and our recommended TTL mapping.
[07:09] Priya: any surprises from last week's run we should be aware of?
[07:12] Samir: we noticed small p99 spikes when cache misses coincided with background checkpointing on the node — we adjusted checkpoint timing and spikes dropped. logging and tracing will help pinpoint that in your 24h run.
[07:25] Tom: regarding fallback policies, if we route to a smaller model variant during high load, what quality delta should we expect?
[07:31] Samir: smaller variant tends to increase F1/accuracy by ~3-7 points depending on task; for chat UX it's often fine if you tune prompts, but for extraction tasks it can drop more. we'll include model-variant regressions in the eval suite for the 24h run.
[07:46] Maya: ok thanks. pricing question — do you offer committed reserved capacity discounts on top of the dedicated pricing sheet?
[07:52] Elena: yes committed monthly/annual contracts reduce unit price significantly. i'll include two scenarios in the worksheet: pay-as-you-go and 12-month reserved with a 25% discount estimate. exact numbers depend on commit level.
[08:05] Priya: last item — is there a way to show tokens/sec/$ in the console per route so product can monitor cost in real time?
[08:11] Jordan: console has per-route token and cost breakdown, and we can add a tokens/sec/$ KPI to the dashboard as a custom widget for your team.
[08:19] Maya: excellent.
[08:21] Elena: recap/next steps: samir runs 24h replay by 10/27, posts CSV and deck by 10/29; elena to update pricing worksheet and share by 10/24; priya to schedule exec review 10/30; tom to send prod sequence distribution by 10/27.
[08:37] Priya: noted. thanks everyone.
[08:40] Tom: thanks all, appreciate it.
[08:42] Maya: thanks.
[08:44] Elena: i'll follow up in email with links: benchmark sheet, security doc, sample SDK TTL config.
[08:50] [call ends]
